client_concurrency.scope: GLOBAL across all OMP processes on this config root, not per session. Proven by inspecting ~/.omp/run/provider-inflight/<provider>/, which held four concurrent lease directories named <pid>-<ts>-<uuid> from three distinct PIDs, coordinated by sibling .lock dirs and .wakeup files.
client_concurrency.why_12: Matches the server's --max-num-seqs 12 so there is ONE authority on concurrency. Raised from 2, which was derived correctly for the old TP=2 pool of 332,475 tokens (2.7 mean prompts fit) and never revisited when the pool grew to 2,653,279 (21.6 fit). At 2 it was throttling 4-10 sessions through a 6x bottleneck, and every load test I ran bypassed OMP so it never showed up.
client_concurrency.if_it_had_been_per_process: 12 x 9 sessions = 108 in flight against a 12-seat server, which is the over-subscription that produced 538 preemptions earlier in this project. Verified it is not.

saturation_behaviour.on_exceeding_cap: queues; does NOT error; does NOT fall back to opencode-go
saturation_behaviour.why: retry.fallbackChains fires on ERRORS. vLLM queues past --max-num-seqs rather than rejecting, and the OMP client cap withholds a lease rather than failing. Saturation therefore appears as latency, not as spillover.
saturation_behaviour.timeout_risk: tools.maxTimeout is 0 (uncapped) and retry.maxDelayMs is 300000, so a deeply queued request waits rather than failing fast.
saturation_behaviour.how_to_get_real_spillover: router/gateway.ts returns 503 once every replica is at maxInflight, and a 503 is an error, so it would trigger the chain and spill to opencode-go. Not deployed; deploying it mid-trial would invalidate the availability measurement.

CORRECTION_volume_and_capacity.what_i_got_wrong: Every cost figure I quoted this session used 302M input tokens/month, derived from 82 main-lane turns/day x 122,835 mean prompt tokens. That counts one prompt per TURN. Billing is per API CALL, and each call re-sends the whole grown context. Measured from 490,104 calls over 27 days in ~/.omp/stats.db the real figure is 101.7B prompt tokens/month. I was wrong by 337x.
CORRECTION_volume_and_capacity.verified_independently: prompt:output 547:1 and cacheRead 97.1% of prompt tokens, both reproduced by direct query, matching WorkloadBaseline's 547:1 and 96.8%. The 181:1 ratio I had been using is not reproducible from the corpus.
CORRECTION_volume_and_capacity.cost_verdict: COST NOW STRONGLY FAVOURS LOCAL, the opposite of what I told him. I said 'cloud-hosted GLM is roughly $30/month, which undercuts cost as a justification'. It is $3,302/month. ~$12k of hardware pays back against cloud GLM in 3.6 months and against frontier API rates in 5 days.
CORRECTION_volume_and_capacity.capacity_verdict: BUT the cluster cannot serve this volume. Three independent methods agree: prefill-only 307% of a month, aggregate-throughput 375%, generation-only 91%. Local can carry roughly 27% of his measured workload; ~73% must spill.
consequences: Fallback rate cannot be near zero. It is structurally ~73%, so the headline KPI I defined will measure capacity shortfall rather than reliability.

opencode-go is unusable as that rung: the spill alone is ~$2,422/mo against a $15 allowance that blocks by default. The metered rung must be Z.ai direct or DeepInfra at the same $0.15/$0.03 list, with no cliff.
GLM emits MORE calls per turn than sol (19.5 vs 11.5 in a paired same-session comparison), so migrating work onto GLM increases token volume rather than reducing it.
The 4th node, and probably more than one, is now a capacity requirement rather than a throughput nicety.
assumptions_stated: local prefix-cache hit rate 90.3% measured lifetime; at cloud's observed 97.1% the prefill duty cycle falls to 92%, still saturated.
prefill 1,240 tok/s and aggregate 1,033 tok/s are this cluster's own gated measurements.
historical volume was produced under effectively unmetered cloud capacity; if he throttles subagent fan-out the requirement drops, but that is a behaviour change, not a capacity fix.

capacity_audit_result.audited_by: WorkloadBaseline, adversarially, at my request; I reproduced every figure
capacity_audit_result.my_27pct_was_pessimistic: I counted cacheWrite as local prefill (double-counts ~1.3%; local records zero cacheWrite on all 1,170 calls) and I priced the advisor as live when it is already disabled. Corrected range reproduces theirs exactly.
capacity_audit_result.denominator_sound: error-stop calls are 3.1% of calls but 0.04% of prompt volume (they fail before prefill); fallback re-sends 0.3-0.4%; compaction re-prefills smaller and recurs locally. Total corrections <=1%, not a 30% term.
capacity_audit_result.THE_REAL_CONSTRAINT: Not throughput. It is KV capacity driving the prefix-cache hit rate. Per-call prompt averages 351K, so the 2.65M pool holds 7.6 concurrent sessions against his 9-session peak. The top of the range evicts, which is precisely why local measures 90.3% hit while the same workload ran 96.8-97.2% on cloud. Hit rate is not a model property here, it is a capacity symptom, and recompute scales as (1-H): 90.3%->96.8% cuts prefill 3x.
capacity_audit_result.recommendation: Four MATCHED nodes. On TP=3 you must choose which constraint to break: MTP costs 913K KV tokens but buys 1.45x generation. TP=4 breaks neither and leaves +22% KV margin over his measured peak. Matched units also avoid the documented NVIDIA forum risk of mixing DGX Spark FE with ASUS Ascent, which degrades the RDMA fabric the whole TP design rests on.
capacity_audit_result.KPI_REDEFINED: Fallback rate was the wrong headline; it would have measured capacity shortfall as unreliability. The headline is now PREFIX-CACHE HIT RATE AS A FUNCTION OF CONCURRENT SESSIONS. The collector already records prefix_cache_queries/hits and kv_cache_usage_perc every 5 minutes, so the week tests the eviction hypothesis directly: if H stays near 96.8% at 9 sessions the cluster is sufficient at TP=3; if it degrades toward 90.3% the fourth node is required, not optional.
capacity_audit_result.quota_arm_disqualified: 512 codex primary polls: 343 ok / 56 warning / 113 exhausted. All 113 carry a SERVER-ISSUED resets_at, which a transport failure cannot fabricate, and the streaks are full-day (18/18, 16/16, 24/24, 24/24, 15/15) with same-day transcript spikes of 111/59/205/120/172 usage-limit errors. Genuine exhaustion, verified against my own failed-probe trap.
capacity_audit_result.reporting_gap: OMP records the local endpoint's cacheRead as zero while TTFT arithmetic implies a 92.8% effective hit. Use the cluster's own counters for KPIs, never OMP's.

kpi_data_hygiene.why: Every row before this is CONTAMINATED by my own bring-up traffic: three cold 790K needle probes with unique nonces (deliberately cache-hostile), plus concurrent load tests at cap 6/12. Those depress the hit rate and must not be read as workload data.
kpi_data_hygiene.sampling_cadence: raised from 5 min to 1 min. A 5-minute instantaneous gauge would almost never catch a 9-session peak, so the KPI's concurrency label was a very loose lower bound. 1 min narrows it; it does not eliminate the gap.

first_signal_and_its_caveat.observed: H falls 97.5% at 1 session -> 93.8% at 3 -> 73.9% at 4 (9 intervals only)
first_signal_and_its_caveat.but: kv_cache_usage_perc is only 23.7% at 4 sessions, so EVICTION CANNOT BE THE CAUSE at that concurrency. The likelier mechanism is prefix DIVERSITY: concurrent distinct sessions share no prefix, and each new session's first call is a cold miss.
first_signal_and_its_caveat.consequence: This partially undercuts my four-node recommendation. More KV fixes eviction; it does not fix prefix diversity. If H degrades with concurrency while KV sits at a quarter full, a fourth node buys margin but not hit rate, and the 33-47% servable share would not improve. The mechanism must be separated before spending on hardware.

kpi_data_hygiene.what_would_settle_it: Run to >=7 concurrent sessions and read kv_cache_usage_perc at the same time. High concurrency WITH high KV usage and falling H = eviction, fourth node helps. High concurrency with LOW KV usage and falling H = prefix diversity, fourth node does not help and the answer is session affinity or fewer, longer-lived sessions.

cache_floor_finding.discovered_while: validating my own eviction discriminator, which read warm_hit 0.0 and would have 'proved' total eviction from a 4,000-word smoke test
cache_floor_finding.rule: the final ~2-3 blocks of 2,304 tokens (~4.6-6.9K tokens) are never committed to the prefix cache. A prompt at or below that tail caches NOTHING.
evidence: 8,015 tok = 3.48 blocks -> 0 cached, warm repeat 0.0% hit
30,014 tok = 13.03 blocks -> 23,040 cached (10 blocks), warm repeat 76.8%
120,016 tok = 52.09 blocks -> 115,200 cached (50 blocks), warm repeat 96.0%
cache_floor_finding.why_it_matters: At his real sizes the tail costs 5.8% at 120K, 2.0% at 351K, 0.9% at 782K, so it is negligible for the workload. But it invalidates any cache measurement taken with small prompts, and the natural warm-turn hit rate at realistic size is ~96%, matching the cloud-era 96.8% almost exactly. That is strong evidence the local 90.3% LIFETIME figure is depressed by cold first-calls, NOT by eviction.
cache_floor_finding.latency_effect: 120K cold 64.6 s -> warm 3.6 s, an 18x saving on the repeat.
instrument_faults_found_and_fixed: prompt_tokens_details is null on this build, so per-request cached_tokens does not exist; the first version of the script read a constant 0.0 and looked like total eviction.

the prefix-cache counters flush a scheduler step behind the HTTP response, so an immediate scrape attributed each wave's hits to the NEXT window and reported cold 0.83 / warm 0.00, exactly inverted. Fixed with a settle delay and validated against a known-good repeat.

eviction_experiment.method: 3/6/9 concurrent synthetic sessions, each a unique 365K prefix (his measured mean context), cold wave then warm wave, per-request and differenced-counter measurement with settle delay. Zero preemptions throughout: pure cache eviction, not queueing.
eviction_experiment.verdict: EVICTED, and it is a CLIFF not a slope. Between 41% and 82% of nominal pool the warm hit collapses 98.6% -> 8.0% -> 0.0%. There is no partial credit: once demand exceeds the pool every prefix is reclaimed, so at 9 sessions a follow-up turn re-prefills all 365K tokens and is SLOWER than the original cold turn (eviction plus contention).
eviction_experiment.mechanism_settled: Eviction, NOT prefix diversity. Diversity would leave warm hits high regardless of pool pressure; they went to exactly zero when demand exceeded it.
eviction_experiment.my_earlier_doubt_was_wrong: I had doubted eviction because kv_cache_usage_perc sat at 23.7% while hit rate fell. That gauge reports ACTIVE usage at scrape time; by then requests have finished and their blocks are freed. It read 6.6% in the very arm where eviction destroyed every prefix. Wrong instrument, third time today.
eviction_experiment.effective_capacity: ~3-4 sessions of his mean context on TP=3, not the 7.3 nominal figure. A resident prefix also needs live prefill space, so the cliff sits at 40-80% of pool, not 100%.

node_answer.TP=3 (2.65M): covers 3-4 sessions at 365K. His p95 is fine; his concurrency is not.
node_answer.TP=4 (3.85M): covers ~5-6. Extends the cliff, does not remove it.
node_answer.covering 9-session peak: needs ~6M tokens, roughly TP=7. Not a purchasable unit count.

eviction_experiment.practical_answer: The lever is not hardware, it is the workload shape. Cap concurrent sessions at 3-4 on TP=3 (98.6% hit, 17.5s follow-ups, this hardware is excellent there) or accept cold re-prefill on every turn beyond the cliff. A fourth node buys margin to ~5-6 sessions, not coverage of the 9-session peak.
eviction_experiment.action: queued: 4/5-session arms to locate the cliff, and 6/9-session arms at 175K to test whether halving context doubles usable sessions (it should if the cliff is capacity-bound).
